transcript.content: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Well, to be honest, I'm here because... it's gotten to the point where other people are actually noticing how I'm moving, and they're pointing it out to me. It's really strange, actually, and kind of embarrassing. Half the time, it's like I'm moving underwater. I'll just be sitting there, and someone will ask me a question, and it just takes me absolutely forever to formulate an answer, or even just to gather the physical energy to stand up out of my chair. It’s like gravity is suddenly turned way up or something, and every little movement is just exhausting. 

But then, on the flip side, when I'm not stuck in the mud like that, I get this completely opposite thing where I just can't stop moving. I'll be pacing back and forth across my apartment, just walking holes in the carpet, and I keep rubbing my hands together over and over. You know how it feels when you work in customer service and you just get off a really bad, stressful call with a screaming customer, and you're trying to physically shake that tense energy off? It's exactly like that. I'm just rubbing my hands and pacing around, and I don't even realize I'm doing it until my roommate asks me what's wrong. So, yeah, it's just this constant extreme of either being completely weighed down or totally wound up, and it's starting to really make me self-conscious, which is why I finally decided I needed to come in and see what's going on.
During these times when you feel 'wound up' and are pacing, do you also find that your thoughts are racing, or that you have significantly less need for sleep than usual?

No, no, it's not like that. I mean, my thoughts aren't racing, not like a million miles an hour or anything. It's more just... I'm just agitated, you know? Like, I'll be pacing back and forth, and I'm just thinking about, I don't know, normal stuff, but I just can't sit still. It's not like my brain is bouncing off the walls, it's just my body. And as for sleep, I actually sleep a lot. Probably too much. When I get into those phases where I feel like I'm moving underwater, like I was saying before, I could easily sleep for twelve, fourteen hours a day if I didn't have to drag myself out of bed for work. And even when I'm pacing and rubbing my hands, I still feel exhausted. It's like a tired, wired feeling, if that makes sense? I'm exhausted, but I can't settle down. So, no, I definitely don't feel like I need less sleep. If anything, I just wish I could get some restful sleep where I actually wake up feeling refreshed, instead of just feeling like I ran a marathon while I was unconscious. Because even when I do sleep, it's just... I don't know, it doesn't help. I just wake up feeling heavy again, or I wake up and immediately start feeling that weird, tense energy creeping back in. So yeah, no racing thoughts and definitely no lack of sleep. I'm actually pretty tired most of the time, to be honest.
Have you experienced these periods of feeling 'weighed down' or 'wound up' in the past, perhaps going back several years, or is this the first time you have ever felt this way?

Well, no, it's definitely not the first time. I mean, it hasn't been happening my whole life or anything like that, but it's been a while now. I've actually been trying to pinpoint exactly when it started, because you know how these things are, they kind of sneak up on you and suddenly you realize, hey, I haven't felt normal in a really long time. But if I really trace it back, I can confidently say it's been going on for about two years and three months. 

I know that sounds really specific, but the reason I know the exact timeline is because it all started right after I got fired from my last customer support job. That whole situation was just a nightmare, honestly. I was working at this call center, and the metrics they expected us to hit were just completely unrealistic. They wanted us to keep call times under three minutes, but also resolve these incredibly complex technical issues that people were calling in about, and you just can't do both, you know? It was this constant pressure cooker, and I was getting written up for things that were completely out of my control. And then, one day, my manager pulls me into this tiny, windowless office and just lets me go. No warning, no severance, just pack your desk and get out. 

It was devastating. I mean, I know it's just customer service, but it was my livelihood, and I had rent to pay and student loans from when I was in college—even though I didn't finish, they still want their money, right? So anyway, it was right after that happened, about two years and three months ago, that I first started noticing this heavy feeling. I remember just lying on my couch for days, feeling like I literally couldn't lift my arms. I thought I was just depressed about losing the job, which makes sense, but then it just never really went away. And then the pacing and the hand-rubbing started a little while after that, like my body was trying to physically process all the stress from the job and the firing, but it just got stuck in this weird loop. So yeah, it's been a solid two years and three months of this constant back-and-forth, ever since that awful day they let me go. I keep hoping it'll just wear off, but it really hasn't.

In the two years and three months since you lost that job, have you ever had a period of at least two months where you felt completely like your old self, without any of these heavy or agitated feelings?

Well, no, not completely like my old self. I mean, it's funny you ask about a two-month period specifically, because I've actually kept a sort of mental log of all this, just trying to figure out if there's a pattern, you know? Like, maybe it's seasonal, or maybe it's tied to my diet, or maybe I'm just losing my mind. But no, there definitely hasn't been a solid two-month block of feeling normal. 

If I really look at the whole timeline, since I got fired two years and three months ago... I'd say the heavy, bogged-down feeling, the depression side of it all, that's been hanging over me for about two years and one month. So, there was maybe a tiny window right at the beginning where I was just in shock, but then the heaviness really set in. And since then, it's just been relentless. I mean, sure, there are days, maybe a week here or there, where it sort of eases up a little bit. Like, I'll wake up and think, "Oh, hey, I actually have the energy to do my laundry today," or, "Maybe I'll actually cook a real meal instead of just eating cereal." But those are so brief. They're just these tiny little gasps of air before I get pulled right back under. 

It's incredibly frustrating, honestly, because every time I get one of those brief periods where it eases up, I think, "Okay, this is it, I'm finally turning a corner, I'm getting back to the guy I used to be." You know, the guy who could actually hold down a job and go out with friends and not feel like a walking zombie. But then, almost as soon as I start feeling hopeful, the gravity turns back up, or the restless pacing starts again, and I'm right back where I started. So, yeah, to answer your question, no two-month breaks. Just about two years and a month of this heavy, exhausting feeling, with only a few fleeting moments where it feels like it might actually be lifting. It's just exhausting, you know? It really takes it out of you to constantly feel like you're fighting your own body and mind just to exist on a basic level.
During these past two years, have you ever experienced a period of at least two weeks where you felt deeply sad, hopeless, or completely lost interest in almost everything you used to enjoy?

Yeah... yeah, absolutely. I mean, the sadness is always kind of there, like I was saying with that heavy feeling, but the losing interest part? That's... honestly, that's the part that really scares me the most, because it feels like losing pieces of who I am. You know, it’s not just a day or two where I don’t feel like doing anything. It’s weeks. Whole months, even, where everything just feels entirely pointless. 

Like, before all this started, I had these things that really anchored me. Sketching, for one. I used to always carry this little black notebook with me everywhere. I’d go to different cafes on my days off—back when I had a normal schedule and a paycheck, anyway—and I’d just sit there for hours. I’d sketch the people, the barista, the street outside... and I’d take all these really detailed coffee notes, too. Like, writing down the flavor profiles, whether it was a single origin or a blend, the acidity, all that stuff. It sounds kind of pretentious, I know, but it was just... it was my thing. Sketching, coffee notes, and weekend hikes used to make me feel like myself. On the weekends, if I wasn’t at a coffee shop, I was out on the trails. I loved getting out of the city, hitting the dirt, just breathing real air and getting my heart rate up in a good way.

But lately? For a long time now, it's just... nothing. I’ll actually try, you know? I’ll tell myself, "Okay, today you’re going to draw, you're going to get out of this funk." And I open the notebook, and I’ve got my pen right there in my hand, or I’ll actually sit down on the edge of the bed and lace up my boots... and I just sit there. I just feel nothing pulling me toward it. There's no spark, no motivation, just this giant, heavy emptiness where my passion used to be. It’s like the volume has been turned all the way down on my entire life. I’ll just stare at the blank page or look at the laces on my boots and think, what’s the point? Why even bother going outside? And that feeling, that total emptiness and hopelessness, it just stretches on and on. Two weeks is definitely a safe bet, because I've gone way longer than that without even making a single mark on a page or stepping foot on a trail. It’s just so incredibly depressing to look at the things that used to bring you joy and just feel completely dead to them. So, yeah, I definitely know exactly what you mean by that. It's been happening a lot.
